opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say no, not yet, though we've made real progress and it's easy to underestimate how much.

It helps to separate a few things that get lumped together under "memory." One is capacity: can the model hold a lot of information in its working context at once? We've moved from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of thousands, even millions, and that's a big deal. You can drop in a whole codebase, a stack of papers, or a long conversation history and the model can actually use it.

But capacity isn't the same as lifelong memory. When I think about what memory means for a person, or for a system that's genuinely useful over months or years, a few properties matter.

The first is selectivity. A long context window is a bit like keeping a perfect transcript of everything and rereading it every time you want to think. That's powerful, but it's not how efficient memory works. Good memory involves compression: deciding what matters, abstracting it, and letting the irrelevant detail fade. I've long believed compression is close to the heart of intelligence, and I think the same is true of memory. Storing everything verbatim isn't a solution; it's a way of postponing the problem.

The second is cost and scaling. Even with clever attention variants and caching, attending over an ever-growing history isn't free. If an agent is going to run for a year, you can't just keep appending to the context forever. At some point you need consolidation into something more durable, whether that's the weights, a structured external store, or some learned compressed representation.

The third is actually using what's in the context. Needle-in-a-haystack tests showed models can retrieve a planted fact from a long document, and that got saturated fairly quickly. But retrieving a single fact is much easier than reasoning across many scattered pieces of information, noticing that something from three weeks ago contradicts something said today, or updating your beliefs because of it. Performance on those harder, multi-hop, long-range reasoning tasks still degrades as context grows. So "it's in the window" and "the model effectively remembers it" aren't the same thing.

And the fourth, which I find the most interesting, is learning versus recall. Lifelong memory for a human isn't just retrieving episodes; it changes you. You get better at things, your intuitions shift, you build skills. Long context gives us something like a very good episodic buffer, but it doesn't by itself give us continual learning, where experience gets folded back into the model's competence. That's a genuinely open research problem, and I don't think anyone has a fully satisfying answer yet.

So my assessment is that long context has largely solved the working-memory side, which is a precondition for everything else and unlocks a lot of practical value right now. The lifelong part, meaning selective, compressed, cheap to maintain, robust to reason over, and actually shaping the model over time, is still very much a frontier. It's one of the areas I'm most excited about, because I think whoever gets it right changes what these systems can be: less a brilliant amnesiac you re-brief every morning, and more a collaborator that genuinely accumulates experience with you.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back on the framing a little, because I think "long context" and "lifelong memory" get conflated and they're really quite different problems.

What we've solved, or at least made enormous progress on, is the ability to attend over a very large window of tokens within a single episode. You can drop a million tokens in and the model can retrieve a needle out of it, do some reasoning across it, and that's genuinely impressive. A few years ago that would have seemed like science fiction. But that's essentially working memory that's been stretched to an extreme. It's expensive, it's recomputed from scratch, and crucially, nothing persists once the context is gone.

Lifelong memory, the way I'd define it, has a few properties that today's systems mostly lack. One is that it's cumulative over very long horizons, months or years, not one session. Two, it's selective. A human doesn't store every sensory input verbatim; there's compression and consolidation and forgetting, and the forgetting is actually a feature, it's what lets you generalise. And three, the memory changes the system. When I learn something today, it alters how I perceive and act tomorrow, it's not just a lookup I do at inference time.

Current approaches mostly bolt on retrieval, you stick things in a vector database and pull them back in, and that gets you a kind of memory, but it's quite brittle. It doesn't know what's worth keeping, it doesn't integrate knowledge, and it tends to retrieve surface-level similarity rather than what's actually relevant. So I'd say we've got a very capable short-term memory and a somewhat clumsy filing cabinet, and the piece in the middle, the consolidation process that turns experience into durable, usable knowledge, is still largely open.

The honest answer is that I don't think we'll know we've solved it until we have systems that get meaningfully better at a particular user's or organisation's problems over months of interaction, without retraining, and I don't think anyone can really claim that yet.

astra-6.text:
I think long context is a really useful step, but I wouldn’t say it solves lifelong memory. It gives you a larger working memory: you can put a lot of information in front of the model and let it reason over that. But a lifetime of experience is still much larger than any context window, and you don’t necessarily want to reread your entire life every time someone asks you a question.

The question is what you retain from an experience, how you organize it, and how you bring the relevant parts back when you need them. Some things you want to remember precisely; other things you want to turn into a more general understanding. And you need to update that understanding when circumstances change.

So I’d assess it over time. Can the model learn something from an interaction and use it appropriately much later, after a lot of unrelated interactions? Can it distinguish an old preference from a new one? Can it connect experiences without being explicitly told which ones to retrieve? Finding a fact in a long context is useful evidence, but it’s a narrower capability than having a memory that makes you a better collaborator over months or years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think long context is a really important step, but I wouldn’t say it solves lifelong memory. It helps to distinguish how much information a model can have in front of it from how well it can learn from an ongoing stream of experience.

Even if you can fit a huge amount of someone’s history into the context, you still need to decide what to retain, how to retrieve it, and how to update it when something changes. And you want the model to use that information reliably. Being able to find a particular sentence in a long document is useful, but it’s a much narrower capability than building an understanding of someone over years.

There’s also a computational question: do we really want to reread our entire life history every time we answer a question? Probably you want some combination of recent context, retrieval, and more compressed, persistent knowledge. Long context gives us a powerful component of that system. The stronger test is whether an agent gets consistently better through experience over long periods, while keeping its knowledge current. I don’t think we’ve demonstrated that just by extending the context window.
